verdicts.trueWording: human-authored text exhibits richer variability in lexical
verdicts.note: Abstract, arxiv.org/abs/2509.18880 (v3, 25 Feb 2026; Comments: accepted to TMLR '26), fetched raw by curl. Quote is word-for-word; the abstract continues 'and structural unpredictability than LLM outputs', so both limbs (lexical and structural) hold. Framing note: the paper states it as the observation motivating DivEye, not as a new measurement of its own.

verdicts.trueWording: resulting in unnaturally flat probability curves devoid of these organic
verdicts.note: Section 3.1 'Design Hypothesis' (confirmed at that section in both the arXiv HTML v3 and the published TMLR PDF, header 'Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (02/2026)'). Quote word-for-word. Both limbs hold: the sentence names likelihood-maximization objectives, the theoretical UID optimum approximated too strictly, and the flat curves as the result. One hedge the claim drops: the paper says LLMs 'often' approximate it too strictly, and it cites Holtzman et al. 2020 rather than measuring this itself.

LOCATOR ERROR IN THE CLAIM'S PAGE FIELD: this is section 4.6 'Ablation Studies', subsection 'Relevance of DivEye's Features' - NOT section 5, which is the two-sentence Conclusion. Verified in the published TMLR PDF (pdf line 768) where the quote renders exactly as given; the arXiv HTML puts 39.4% in a math element so it extracts with spaces. Both comparison limbs hold: distributional features follow at 34.2% and first-order differences at 23.7%. The figures are averaged feature importances from a trained XGBoost model.

verdicts.trueWording: outperforms existing zero-shot detectors by up to 33.2%
verdicts.note: Abstract. The claim's own quote ('pointing to rhythmic unpredictability as a powerful and') is separately word-for-word in the same abstract, and the 33.2% limb is stated in the sentence given as trueWording. Scope note the claim omits: the abstract pairs this with 'competitive performance with fine-tuned baselines', so the 33.2% is against zero-shot detectors only, which is what the claim says.

verdicts.trueWording: 50-50 chance of guessing whether a piece of sample
verdicts.note: Section 'Who will identify AI content?', WhatamIdoing, 23:34, 4 September 2026, on en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Wikivoyage_talk:AI_guidelines (raw wikitext via ?action=raw). Quote word-for-word (the page uses an en dash in 50-50). 'Recalled a study' is exact: 'There was a study a while ago that said'. The 'experienced Wikimedia policy editor' limb is supported on the same page but in a different section - in 'Assistive technology' the same editor writes of having a lot of experience with policy writing (01:33, 5 September 2026). The editor also says he/she is bad at detecting AI use and possibly worse than 50-50.

Same comment, same section and timestamp as 1149. Quote word-for-word. FLAG, not buried: the page states no gender for User:WhatamIdoing, so the pronoun 'he' is the claim's own attribution and is not supported by the source - drop the pronoun downstream. Second wording gap: the page calls what was found 'something unencyclopedically puffy', not 'a passage'. Everything else holds - English Wikipedia, suspected AI-generated, discovered via a trip through the page history - and the page adds that 22 years is about 19 years before AI text generators were generally available.

verdicts.trueWording: claiming a particular beach resort has a restaurant because many do
verdicts.note: Section 'Hallucinations', User:LPfi/AI guidelines (raw wikitext; page carries {{experimental}}; current revision 2026-09-03, so 'revision of September 2026' is right). Quote word-for-word. The 'substituting the typical for the particular' clause is the claim's own gloss rather than the draft's wording, but it is entailed by the example as written (a particular resort, inferred from what many resorts have). The draft's own label for these is 'AI hallucinations'.

verdicts.trueWording: avoid converting an article into an obvious AI voice
verdicts.note: Section heading is exactly 'AI assisted copy editing' on User:LPfi/AI guidelines. Quote word-for-word. The 'existing article' limb is supported: the paragraph opens 'For existing articles, you shouldn't get carried away' and the same sentence tells editors to aim to maintain the original tone and style.

verdicts.trueWording: some average or mishmash of the inputs
verdicts.note: Section 'Copyright issues', User:LPfi/AI guidelines. Quote word-for-word. The 'large language model' limb is supported two sentences earlier in the same section, which describes current AI programs as applying a large language model to a collection of inputs. The draft's sentence ends 'that is not what Wikivoyage needs'.

verdicts.trueWording: do not use the style AI chatbots tend to use
verdicts.note: Section 'Discussions', User:LPfi/AI guidelines. Quote word-for-word. Both limbs hold, but name the carve-out downstream: the bar is on AI tools in talk-page posts 'other than for spelling correction, finding a word, and similar tasks', and the draft adds that the original wording must be the editor's and that pace and volume should match unassisted participation.

verdicts.trueWording: there were 102 mentions of food poisoning at the Riu Palace
verdicts.note: Which? press release, 02 Jul 2026, fetched raw by curl (server-rendered HTML, no summarizer). Quote word-for-word. Two limbs rest on nearby context rather than the sentence itself: the sentence says 'checked in March this year', and 2026 comes from the article's own 02 Jul 2026 dateline; and 'guest reviews' comes from the preceding paragraph, which is about recent guest reviews on Tripadvisor. The hotel is introduced earlier as the five-star all-inclusive Riu Palace Santa Maria in Cape Verde. Same paragraph adds 32 one- and two-star reviews Dec 2025-Apr 2026, 14 reporting illness.

Kaia Coracesium section of the Which? release. Quote word-for-word including the bracketed insertion (the page uses curly quotes). Limbs hold: several reviewers who visited last summer wrote they felt unsafe due to repeated sexual harassment from male hotel staff. Framing the claim compresses: the article says the summary describes the service as 'friendly' and that this phrase is the closest it comes to referring to those allegations, rather than saying it rendered the reports as that phrase.

verdicts.trueWording: the language used appears to minimise their significance
verdicts.note: Paragraph immediately after the Kaia Coracesium example. Quote word-for-word, and the 'where the summaries do reference serious allegations' limb matches the article's 'when they do'. One framing gap worth carrying: Which? puts it as a question that remains open - why such references do not appear consistently and why, when they do, the language appears to minimise - rather than as a flat conclusion. The preceding sentence says the AI systems are evidently capable of identifying and referencing such allegations.

verdicts.trueWording: identify the most common themes and then turn those themes
verdicts.note: Tripadvisor's statement quoted in the Which? release. The claim's 12-word quote is word-for-word; the statement's full clause has the summaries use large language models and natural language processing to read recent reviews before that phrase, which supports the claim's 'the models' limb, and ends with short, plain-English overviews. Tripadvisor adds that summaries update monthly over the previous 12 months of reviews and that reviews are treated equally regardless of rating.

verdicts.trueWording: Google manages context in their AI summaries far better
verdicts.note: Comparison-with-rival-platforms section of the Which? release. Quote word-for-word (present tense 'manages'; the claim's past tense is reported speech). The 'of the same hotel warning of potential for illness' limb is the next sentence: Google's overview for the Riu Palace warned of 'potential for illness' and flagged outbreaks of illness and concerns over birds in the buffet areas. The 'than Tripadvisor' comparator is implicit - the sentence names no comparator, but it opens a paragraph framed as Which? looking at a rival platform's approach, in an article wholly about Tripadvisor.
